analysis.one_liner: Imposes staffing, transparency, and arbitration rules on nursing homes caring for Medicare and Medicaid patients.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee in September 2021 and never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nursing homes serving Medicare and Medicaid residents to have a registered nurse on site 24 hours a day, provided infection-control services, and met minimum staff-to-resident ratios set by federal regulators. It would also have barred nursing homes from forcing residents into pre-dispute arbitration agreements, required facilities to post surety bonds, audited facility cost reports, penalized facilities that report inaccurate staffing data, and sent new federal Medicaid money to states to raise nursing home staff wages. The bill went to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, then to a Health Subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who would get more nurse coverage, stronger infection control, honest staffing data, and the right to sue in court rather than being pushed into arbitration. Nursing home workers would benefit from a temporary boost in federal Medicaid matching funds tied to higher staff wages and benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and care workers

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires skilled nursing facilities to have a registered professional nurse on duty 24 hours a day, 7 days a week beginning October 1, 2023, and infection control services overseen by an infection preventionist for at least 40 hours per week.
It directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to study and then set minimum staff-to-resident ratios for nursing staff, with facilities required to comply, subject to limited rural waivers.

It prohibits nursing homes and home health or home care providers from entering into or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements with residents, preserving residents' right to take abuse or neglect claims to court.

It imposes civil penalties of up to $10,000 per submission on facilities that report inaccurate staffing data, requires a surety bond of at least $500,000 from facilities, and requires annual audits of nursing home cost reports.

It temporarily raises the federal Medicaid matching rate for states that use the extra money to raise nursing home staff wages and benefits, improve payment rates, and expand training, with reporting and an independent evaluation required.
It expands the Special Focus Facility program to cover at least 5 percent of nursing facilities and funds on-site consultation and educational programming for persistently poor-performing facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, particularly for-profit chains, would bear the cost of higher staffing levels, surety bonds, audit exposure, and penalties. The arbitration industry would lose the pre-dispute arbitration business that nursing home admission contracts generate. Taxpayers fund the oversight through transfers from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund and direct appropriations, including $250 million for cost report audits and $1.3 billion for a building-modification and staff-investment demonstration program.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and Medicare trust funds

drawbacks.text: Higher mandatory staffing levels raise operating costs for facilities already running on thin margins, which can be passed to private-pay residents or push marginal facilities, especially in rural areas, to close; the bill's own rural waiver provisions acknowledge that staffing mandates could worsen the supply of nursing home care in some areas.

The staffing ratio requirement was not immediate: the Secretary would first have to complete a study (due up to three years after enactment) and then issue regulations up to two years later, so binding ratios would arrive years down the road.

The bill costs federal money, including transfers from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund of $250 million for cost report audits, $50 million for the staffing study, and $30 million for the demonstration program administration, plus a $1.3 billion appropriation for the demonstration program itself.

Raising the federal Medicaid matching rate for nursing facility services channels substantial new federal spending through nursing facilities as they exist today, which can entrench current operators rather than funding home- and community-based alternatives, though the bill also funds options counseling on non-institutional care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits — 24-hour registered nurse coverage, accurate staffing data, and a ban on forced arbitration for frail elderly residents — directly address documented problems in nursing home care, and the costs fall mainly on facility operators rather than residents. The main weaknesses are design and timing: binding staffing ratios would take years to materialize, rural supply risks are real enough that the bill builds in waivers, and a large share of the new money flows through existing facilities rather than toward alternatives to institutional care. On balance it is a consumer- and worker-protective bill with real but manageable costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to a Health Subcommittee the day it was introduced, and no committee or subcommittee ever voted on it before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal introduced the bill with Rep. Frank Pallone on September 3, 2021.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Within days it was further referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
Four Democratic members cosponsored the bill; no Republicans cosponsored it.
No markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off because the bill died: no new staffing minimums, surety bond, cost report audits, or arbitration ban ever took effect, and residents' conditions were left unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators, who kept the status quo

for.name: Richard E. Neal
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MA), Chair of the House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it within his own committee, which took no further action on it.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-NJ), Chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill, which was referred to his committee and never advanced there.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred to it and its Health Subcommittee; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Nursing home industry
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed mandatory federal staffing minimums and pressed Congress to pair any nursing home rules with new federal funding instead.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators (skilled nursing and nursing facilities)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed 24-hour registered nurse coverage, minimum staffing ratios, surety bonds, cost report audits, penalties for inaccurate staffing data, and a ban on forced arbitration, all of which raise operating costs for an industry that profits by keeping staffing low. Many facilities are owned by for-profit chains, where staffing savings flow directly to owners.

industries.industry: Nursing home care workforce (nurses and aides)
industries.note: The bill would have raised staff wages and benefits through a temporary increase in federal Medicaid matching funds, and required more nurses per facility. Its wage and reporting provisions would also have increased job transparency.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and nursing home legal defense
industries.note: Nursing home admission contracts routinely force residents into pre-dispute arbitration, keeping abuse and neglect claims out of court. The bill would have barred those agreements for nursing homes and home care providers.

The bill appropriates $570 million for survey improvements and directs that on-site compliance assistance for poor-performing facilities be carried out by quality improvement organizations, creating funded work for them.
